lead: A quotient space glues together vectors that differ only by a subspace W. The result is a new vector space V/W whose points are cosets v+W. This idea exists because many questions care about a vector only up to a harmless shift inside W: in R², all points on the same horizontal line differ by a point on the x-axis. Only a few universities teach this topic. It is used in linear algebra proofs and in error-correcting codes.
prereq: You need: vector spaces, subspaces, linear independence, and basis and dimension.

blocks.text: Fix a vector space V and a subspace W. For a vector v in V, the coset v+W is the set of all vectors v+w with w in W. Two vectors lie in the same coset exactly when their difference lies in W. The quotient space V/W is the set of all cosets. Its zero is W itself, because 0+W=W. The negative of v+W is −v+W.

blocks.where: v is a vector in V; W is a subspace; w runs over W; V/W is the quotient space.

blocks.text: The operations on V/W are (u+W)+(v+W)=(u+v)+W and a(v+W)=av+W. They are well defined. If u+W=u′+W and v+W=v′+W, then u−u′∈W and v−v′∈W. Hence (u+v)−(u′+v′)=(u−u′)+(v−v′)∈W, so the sum is the same for every choice of representatives. Also av−av′=a(v−v′)∈W, so the scalar product is independent of the representative.
For finite-dimensional V, dim V/W = dim V − dim W. The quotient map sends each v to v+W; its kernel is W.

The replacement theorem, also called Steinitz exchange, compares a basis with an independent set. Let B={v₁,...,v_n} be a basis of V and let I={u₁,...,u_m} be an independent set. Then m≤n. After reordering B, some m of its vectors can be replaced by u₁,...,u_m and the result is still a basis.

Proof by exchange. Add u₁ to B. The enlarged set is dependent, so u₁ is a non-zero combination of B; some basis vector v_i has non-zero coefficient. Remove v_i. The new set spans V and has n vectors, so it is a basis. Repeat for u₂,...,u_m. Independence makes the next u_j lie outside the span of the earlier u's, so a basis vector with non-zero coefficient remains to remove.

Two consequences follow. The deletion theorem: a finite spanning set S contains a basis; delete one vector at a time while the span stays the same. The extension theorem: an independent set in a finite-dimensional space can be grown to a basis; add vectors until maximal. Also, any two bases have the same size: replacement gives m≤n and n≤m.

figure.caption: The x-axis is collapsed to zero, so all points on a horizontal line y=b become one point of V/W. The quotient has dimension 2−1=1.

spec.aria: Collapsing the x-axis makes each horizontal line of the plane one point, and the result is a line.

examples.question: Let V=R² and W=span{(1,0)}, the x-axis. (a) Describe the coset (a,b)+W. (b) State when (a,b)+W=(a′,b′)+W. (c) Find dim V/W and check dim V/W=dim V−dim W.
steps: W consists of all (x,0) with x∈R. Thus (a,b)+W={(a+x,b):x∈R}, the horizontal line y=b.
Two cosets are equal exactly when (a,b)−(a′,b′)=(a−a′,b−b′) lies in W. This happens exactly when b−b′=0, so b=b′.
The map f((a,b)+W)=b is well defined by step 2. It is one-to-one: equal b means equal cosets. It is onto R: b comes from (0,b)+W.
dim W=1, because W is spanned by one non-zero vector. dim V=2. Hence dim V/W=dim V−dim W=2−1=1.
examples.answer: The coset is the horizontal line y=b; cosets are equal exactly when b=b′; dim V/W=1, which equals 2−1.
examples.check:
dimV = 2
dimW = 1
dimQuot = dimV - dimW
print(dimV)
print(dimW)
print(dimQuot)

traps: Adding cosets through different representatives needs proof; the sum is independent only because u−u′∈W and v−v′∈W imply (u+v)−(u′+v′)∈W.
The dimension formula is dim V/W = dim V − dim W, not dim W and not dim V + dim W.
The zero of V/W is W = 0+W, not the zero vector of V.
A coset v+W is a subspace only when v∈W; otherwise it misses the zero vector.

quiz.q: Define the coset v+W and state the zero of V/W.
Why is well-definedness needed for addition in V/W?
quiz.a: A coset has many representatives; the rule must give the same coset for all choices.

quiz.q: In V=R³, W=span{(0,0,1)}. Describe (a,b,c)+W and find dim V/W.
quiz.a: It is the vertical line {(a,b,z):z∈R}; dim V/W=3−1=2.

quiz.q: If a space has a basis of 4 vectors, can five vectors be independent? Use replacement.
quiz.a: No. Replacement gives m≤4, so five independent vectors contradict m≤n.

quiz.q: In V=R², W=span{(0,1)}. Describe (a,b)+W and when two such cosets are equal.
quiz.a: Vertical line x=a; equality holds exactly when a=a′.

quiz.q: State the deletion theorem and the extension theorem.
quiz.a: Deletion: a finite spanning set contains a basis. Extension: an independent set extends to a basis.

beyond: Not for the exam. Quotient spaces become quotient modules in abstract algebra and appear in coding theory, where messages equal up to a codeword are identified. In control theory, quotient spaces describe systems that ignore unobservable states. Search for quotient vector space, Steinitz exchange lemma and quotient module.
